[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mastering Window Functions and Analytical Queries in Apache Spark"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Window functions in Apache Spark SQL allow you to perform calculations across a set of table rows that are somehow related to the current row. Unlike standard aggregate functions that group rows into a single output row, window functions retain the original rows while appending the calculated analytical result."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding the Anatomy of a Window Function"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"A window specification defines how the data is partitioned and ordered before the function is applied. It consists of three primary components: Partitioning (PARTITION BY), Ordering (ORDER BY), and Framing (ROWS BETWEEN)."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"PARTITION BY: Splits the data into logical groups, similar to GROUP BY, but without collapsing the rows."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"ORDER BY: Determines the logical sequence of rows within each partition."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Frame Clause: Specifies the subset of rows relative to the current row that form the evaluation window."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Setting Up the Spark Session"},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder \
    .appName("SparkWindowFunctionsTutorial") \
    .getOrCreate()"},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Creating Sample Data"},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"data = [
    ("Engineering", "Alice", 85000),
    ("Engineering", "Bob", 90000),
    ("Engineering", "Charlie", 95000),
    ("Sales", "David", 75000),
    ("Sales", "Eve", 80000),
    ("Sales", "Frank", 85000)
]

columns = ["Department", "Employee", "Salary"]
df = spark.createDataFrame(data, columns)
df.createOrReplaceTempView("employees")"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Ranking Functions"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Ranking functions like row_number(), rank(), and dense_rank() assign sequential integers to rows within a partition based on the ORDER BY clause."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"from pyspark.sql.window import Window
import pyspark.sql.functions as F

windowSpec = Window.partitionBy("Department").orderBy(F.col("Salary").desc())

ranked_df = df.withColumn("rank", F.rank().over(windowSpec)) \
              .withColumn("dense_rank", F.dense_rank().over(windowSpec)) \
              .withColumn("row_num", F.row_number().over(windowSpec))

ranked_df.show()"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Analytical Functions: Lead and Lag"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"The lag() and lead() functions allow access to data from a previous or subsequent row, respectively, within the same partition. This is extremely useful for calculating time-series differences, growth rates, or session gaps."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"timeWindow = Window.partitionBy("Department").orderBy("Salary")

comparison_df = df.withColumn("prev_salary", F.lag("Salary", 1).over(timeWindow)) \
                  .withColumn("salary_diff", F.col("Salary") - F.col("prev_salary"))

comparison_df.show()"},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Using Spark SQL for Window Operations"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can achieve the exact same analytical power using pure SQL by utilizing the OVER clause."},{"order":20,"type":"code","text":"spark.sql("""
    SELECT 
        Department,
        Employee,
        Salary,
        AVG(Salary) OVER(PARTITION BY Department) as avg_dept_salary
    FROM employees
""").show()"},{"order":21,"type":"subheading","text":"Performance Considerations"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Window functions require Spark to shuffle data across the cluster to ensure all rows belonging to the same partition reside on the same executor. To optimize performance, ensure your partition keys have high enough cardinality to distribute the workload evenly, and avoid unnecessary sorting operations."}]
